# 1. Paper Overview

- **Title:** GaussianEditor: Swift and Controllable 3D Editing with Gaussian Splatting
- **Authors:** Yiwen Chen\*¹,², Zilong Chen\*³,⁵, Chi Zhang², Feng Wang³, Xiaofeng Yang², Yikai Wang³, Zhongang Cai⁴, Lei Yang⁴, Huaping Liu³, Guosheng Lin\*\*¹,² (\*equal contribution; \*\*corresponding author)
- **Affiliations:** ¹S-Lab / ²School of Computer Science and Engineering, Nanyang Technological University; ³Department of Computer Science and Technology, Tsinghua University; ⁴SenseTime Research; ⁵ShengShu
- **Venue / Version:** arXiv:2311.14521v4 [cs.CV], 20 Dec 2023
- **Project page:** https://buaacyw.github.io/gaussian-editor

## 1.1 Problem Statement

The paper targets 3D scene editing (e.g., text-guided editing of appearance and content, object removal, object insertion). Two existing families of 3D representations are argued to be inadequate:

1. **Traditional explicit representations** (meshes, point clouds): allow interactive editing but "often fall short in realistically depicting complex scenes" (Abstract).
2. **Implicit representations (NeRF)**: render complex scenes with high fidelity but are slow and provide limited control over specific scene regions; their MLP-based encoding restricts direct modification of scene parts, complicates inpainting/scene composition, and slows training/rendering (Sec. 1).

The authors adopt **3D Gaussian Splatting (GS)** [15], chosen for its real-time rendering and explicit, point-cloud-like representation (Sec. 1). They identify two core challenges of editing GS:

- **Challenge 1 — target identification:** there is no efficient method to accurately identify the Gaussians to edit, which is essential for precise, controllable editing (Sec. 1).
- **Challenge 2 — instability under generative guidance:** optimizing GS with highly random generative guidance (e.g., Score Distillation Sampling, SDS [36]) is difficult (observed in [7, 44, 52]). Unlike implicit representations "buffered by neural networks," GS is directly exposed to loss randomness and updates a vast number of Gaussian points per step without neural-network-style moderation, causing unstable updates and hindering convergence to fine details (Sec. 1; Sec. 4.2).

## 1.2 Core Idea and Claims

GaussianEditor is presented as "a novel, swift, and highly controllable 3D editing algorithm for Gaussian Splatting" that can fulfill high-quality editing within minutes (Sec. 1). It has three pillars:

1. **Gaussian semantic tracing** — dynamic, per-Gaussian semantic tags that track the editing target throughout training (Sec. 4.1).
2. **Hierarchical Gaussian Splatting (HGS)** — a generational organization of Gaussians that constrains older generations and frees newer ones, moderating GS fluidity under stochastic guidance (Sec. 4.2).
3. **A dedicated 3D inpainting algorithm for GS** — supporting swift object removal and object incorporation (Sec. 4.3).

**Stated key advantage:** a single editing session takes only 5–10 minutes, with precise, localized edits (Fig. 1 caption: "only the desired parts are modified" — e.g., in "Make the grass on fire," the bench and tree remain unaffected).

## 1.3 Contributions (as enumerated by the authors, Sec. 1)

1. Introduced **Gaussian semantic tracing**, enabling more detailed and effective editing control.
2. Proposed **Hierarchical Gaussian Splatting (HGS)**, a GS representation that converges more stably to refined results under highly random generative guidance.
3. Designed a **3D inpainting algorithm for Gaussian Splatting** allowing swift object removal and addition.
4. Extensive experiments demonstrating superiority over previous 3D editing methods in effectiveness, speed, and controllability.

## 1.4 Reported Limitation

The method inherits the reliance of 2D-diffusion-based 3D editing on the guidance quality of 2D diffusion models; "current 2D diffusion models struggle to offer effective guidance for certain complex prompts, leading to limitations in 3D editing" (Sec. 6, Limitation).

# 2. Background and Related Work

## 2.1 3D Representations (Sec. 2.1)

- **NeRF [28]** popularized implicit neural fields with volumetric rendering, enabling 3D optimization from 2D supervision, but optimization is time-consuming despite wide use in reconstruction [3, 6, 13, 21] and generation [22, 35].
- Acceleration efforts [29, 40] mostly target the *reconstruction* setting; the common spatial-pruning technique does not effectively speed up the *generation* setting.
- **3D Gaussian Splatting [15]** has emerged as an alternative, demonstrating impressive quality and speed in 3D/4D reconstruction [15, 26, 47, 50, 51] and attracting interest in generation [7, 44, 52]. Its efficient differentiable rendering and design avoid the need for spatial pruning.
- The paper claims to be the first to adapt 3D Gaussian Splatting to 3D editing tasks (Sec. 2.1).

## 2.2 3D Editing (Sec. 2.2)

Prior work is organized into several lines:

- **Latent-code-conditioned field editing:** EditNeRF [24] edits shape and color by conditioning neural fields on latent codes.
- **CLIP-guided editing:** works such as [1, 10, 45, 46] use CLIP models to drive editing via text prompts or reference images.
- **Template/skeleton-based:** [30, 33] use predefined template models or skeletons for re-posing/re-rendering within specific categories.
- **Geometry-based:** [20, 48, 49, 54] convert neural fields to meshes and synchronize mesh deformation with implicit fields.
- **2D-manipulation + field training:** combining 2D image manipulation (e.g., inpainting) with neural field training [19, 23].
- **Static-mask-constrained editing:** concurrent works [31, 57] use static 2D/3D masks to constrain the edit area of NeRF. **Key critique:** 3D model training is a dynamic process; static masks cannot effectively constrain it because the geometries and appearances of 3D models evolve during training (Sec. 2.2, Sec. 4.1). Additionally, static masks "lock" edited content within a fixed spatial boundary, preventing natural expansion beyond the mask (Sec. 4.1).
- **Semantic NeRF [56]** improves this only marginally: gradient control is effective only at the very beginning of training, since ongoing NeRF updates degrade semantic-field accuracy (Sec. 4.1).

## 2.3 Diffusion-based Editing Guidance (Sec. 3.2)

The paper does not design new guidance mechanisms; it directly employs existing 2D diffusion guidance. Two broad categories:

1. **SDS-style scoring (e.g., Dreamfusion [36]):** feed the noised rendering of the current 3D model plus conditions into a 2D diffusion model [39]; the diffusion scores guide model updates [8, 27, 31, 36, 42, 57].
2. **2D-edit-then-train:** apply prompt-based 2D editing to multiview renderings of the 3D model, producing a multi-view 2D image dataset used as training target [5, 12, 37, 43].

Both types are compatible with GaussianEditor. The guidance is abstracted as an operator **D**; the edit loss is written generically as:

> L_Edit = D(Θ; p, e)   (Eq. 5)

where Θ are the 3D model parameters, p the rendered camera pose, and e the prompt (Sec. 3.2).

## 2.4 Positioning

GaussianEditor differentiates itself by (a) pioneer adaptation of GS to 3D editing, (b) dynamic (tracing) rather than static masks, and (c) a generational (HGS) representation to stabilize GS under stochastic generative guidance. Baselines used later are Instruct-Nerf2Nerf [12] and GaussianEditor variants with delta denoising score (DDS) [14] guidance (Fig. 5).

# 3. Methodology Analysis

## 3.1 Preliminaries: 3D Gaussian Splatting (Sec. 3.1)

Each Gaussian is defined by a center point (mean) x and covariance matrix Σ, with the Gaussian function:

> G(x) = e^(−½ xᵀΣ⁻¹x)   (Eq. 1)

Σ is decomposed into rotation R and scaling S for differentiable optimization:

> Σ = R S Sᵀ Rᵀ   (Eq. 2)

For novel-view rendering, splatting [53, 58] positions Gaussians on camera planes via viewing transformation W and Jacobian J of the affine approximation of the projective transform, giving the camera-space covariance:

> Σ′ = J W Σ Wᵀ Jᵀ   (Eq. 3)

Each Gaussian is parameterized by position x ∈ ℝ³, color via spherical-harmonics coefficients c ∈ ℝᵏ (k = degrees of freedom), opacity α ∈ ℝ, rotation quaternion q ∈ ℝ⁴, and scaling s ∈ ℝ³. Pixel color/opacity are computed by alpha-blending over N ordered overlapping points:

> C = Σ_{i∈N} cᵢ αᵢ Π_{j=1}^{i−1} (1 − αⱼ)   (Eq. 4)

where cᵢ, αᵢ are the color and density of point i (Sec. 3.1). **Note:** the paper's reference list numbers GS as [15] in the body (and as [16]/[17] in different contexts), all pointing to the same Kerbl et al. ToG 2023 paper.

## 3.2 Task Definition (Sec. 4)

Given a prompt y and a GS scene Θ with each Θᵢ = {xᵢ, sᵢ, qᵢ, αᵢ, cᵢ}, the goal is to produce an edited 3D Gaussian scene Θ_y that adheres to prompt y.

## 3.3 Component 1: Gaussian Semantic Tracing (Sec. 4.1)

**Motivation.** Static 2D/3D masks (used by [31, 57]) become inaccurate as the 3D representation changes during training; even semantic NeRF [56] loses accuracy quickly. Because GS is explicit, semantic labels can be attached directly to each Gaussian, enabling "semantic tracing in 3D scenes."

**Mechanism.**
- A new attribute **m** is added to each Gaussian: mᵢⱼ is the semantic mask of the i-th Gaussian for the j-th semantic label.
- **Label acquisition via unprojection:** multi-view renderings I of Θ are processed by a 2D segmentation method [18] (SAM) to obtain 2D masks M. For each pixel p, the semantic label is unprojected back to the Gaussians affecting it using inverse rendering:

> wⁱⱼ = Σ_p oᵢ(p) · Tⁱⱼ(p) · Mⱼ(p)   (Eq. 6)

  where wⁱⱼ is the weight of the i-th Gaussian for the j-th semantic label, oᵢ(p) the opacity, Tⁱⱼ(p) the transmittance from pixel p, and Mⱼ(p) the semantic mask of pixel p. A Gaussian is assigned to the j-th class if its average weight exceeds a manually set threshold (Sec. 4.1).
- **Dynamic tracking:** during densification, newly densified points inherit the semantic label of their parent, so an accurate 3D semantic mask exists at every moment of training (Sec. 4.1). The mask m functions as a *dynamic* 3D segmentation mask that evolves with training and allows content to expand freely in space — in contrast to NeRF, where content is restricted to a fixed spatial area.
- **Speed:** the labeling process typically takes less than a second.
- **Applications enabled:** manually changing colors/moving properties of a category, deleting categories, and independently rendering small objects for more precise 2D-diffusion supervision (Sec. 4.1).

**Assessment.** Strengths: the inheritance rule keeps masks consistent through densification/pruning; editing can be restricted to target Gaussians only, addressing the "identify target" challenge. Weaknesses: the classification threshold is manual and its value is not reported; quality depends on the 2D segmentation quality (paper acknowledges inaccurate initial masks are still workable thanks to tracing, Fig. 2 caption); no quantitative evaluation of segmentation accuracy is provided.

## 3.4 Component 2: Hierarchical Gaussian Splatting (HGS) (Sec. 4.2)

**Motivation.** Vanilla GS works well for reconstruction due to SFM [41] point-cloud initialization and stable ground-truth supervision, but under generative guidance the randomness of the loss is directly applied to a large number of points each step, without neural-network-like memorization/moderating ability, causing erratic updates and over-fluidity that prevents convergence to details (Sec. 4.2).

**Mechanism.**
- **Generations by densification round:** initial Gaussians are generation 0; points produced in the k-th densification round are marked generation k.
- **Anchor loss:** at training start, HGS records the attributes of all Gaussians as anchors; anchors are updated to the current state at each densification process. An MSE loss between anchor and current states prevents Gaussians from deviating too far:

> L_anchor^P = Σ_{i=0}^{n} λᵢ (Pᵢ − P̂ᵢ)²   (Eq. 7)

  where n is the number of Gaussians, P a property from {x, s, q, α, c}, P̂ the anchor-state property, and λᵢ the per-Gaussian anchor-loss strength varying by generation.
- **Total loss:**

> L = L_Edit + Σ_{P∈{x,s,q,α,c}} λ_P · L_anchor^P   (Eq. 8)

  with λ_P the strength per property and L_Edit the edit loss of Eq. 5.
- **Generational constraint schedule:** with each densification, the anchor weight λᵢ of *all previous generations* is increased, so older generations' fluidity decreases until nearly solidified; the almost-unconstrained new-generation Gaussians carve out details. This "simulates the buffering function achieved in implicit representations through neural networks" (Sec. 1).
- **Controllability of constraints:** increasing generation-0 anchor weight limits changes to the original GS; stronger anchor loss on specific properties prevents changing those properties (Sec. 4.2).
- **Densification criterion:** instead of a manually set threshold, HGS densifies only the Gaussians whose 3D position gradients are within the top k% at each densification step (percentage criterion, more manageable and intuitive) (Sec. 4.2).

**Assessment.** Strengths: conceptually simple (a generation-indexed anchor regularization) and directly addresses the documented instability of GS under SDS-like losses; the property-wise and generation-wise weighting gives intuitive knobs. Weaknesses: no concrete values for λᵢ, λ_P, or k% are given anywhere in the paper; anchors being re-recorded at each densification weakens the theoretical guarantee of "preserving original state"; the paper provides only qualitative ablations (Fig. 7), with no quantitative metric for convergence stability.

## 3.5 Component 3: 3D Inpainting for GS (Sec. 4.3)

### Object Removal
- Simply deleting Gaussians identified by a mask creates artifacts at object–scene interfaces.
- **Boundary mask refinement:** after deletion, KNN identifies Gaussians nearest to the removed ones (likely at interfaces); these are projected onto views; the mask is dilated and holes fixed to accurately represent the interface area.
- **Supervision:** a repaired image is generated with a 2D inpainting method and used with **MSE loss** for supervision (Fig. 4 caption).
- **Time:** the whole object-removal procedure takes ~2 minutes.

### Object Incorporation
- Task definition: given 3D Gaussians θ, a camera pose p with rendering I, a user-provided 2D mask M on I, and a prompt y, update θ to fulfill the inpainting request.
- **Pipeline:**
  1. Generate a 2D inpainted image I^M_y via a 2D inpainting diffusion model [34] (SDXL).
  2. Segment the foreground object from I^M_y and feed it to an image-to-3D method [25] (Wonder3D) to get a coarse 3D mesh.
  3. Convert the mesh to 3D Gaussians θ_y and refine with HGS (Sec. 4.2).
  4. **Coordinate alignment:** estimate the depth of I^M_y [38] (DPT), align it with the depth map rendered by θ at pose p via **least squares**; determine the coordinate and scale of the foreground object in θ's coordinate system.
  5. Transform θ_y into θ's coordinate system and **concatenate** the Gaussians.
- **Time:** ~3 min for mesh generation + ~2 min for GS conversion/refinement; composition takes <1 second; total ~5 minutes (Sec. 4.3, Sec. 5.1).

**Assessment.** Strengths: pragmatic pipeline reusing strong off-the-shelf components (SDXL inpainting, Wonder3D, DPT); avoids optimizing a single fused scene by direct concatenation after alignment, which explains the speed. Weaknesses: dependence on monocular depth estimation can produce misaligned objects (acknowledged in Appendix C.2, addressed by manual webUI scale adjustment); foreground segmentation and image-to-3D failures propagate into the final composition; no quantitative evaluation of alignment quality or inpainting fidelity.

## 3.6 Overall Framework Assessment

- **Novelty:** the combination of explicit per-Gaussian semantic labels with a generational anchor-loss representation is a coherent and original response to the two identified GS-editing challenges; the inpainting pipeline is engineering-oriented but effective.
- **Theoretical grounding:** the paper is empirical; no formal guarantees are given for HGS convergence or semantic tracing accuracy.
- **Abstraction of guidance:** using any off-the-shelf 2D guidance (Eq. 5) makes the framework modular (demonstrated with both iN2N and DDS), which is a plus for generality.
- **Reporting gaps:** hyperparameters (λᵢ, λ_P, k%, segmentation threshold, learning rates, loss weights) are not reported; the quantitative evaluation is thin (one table with two metrics, no PSNR/SSIM, no dataset specification, no error bars or statistics for the user study).

# 4. Experiments and Results

## 4.1 Implementation Details (Sec. 5.1)

- **Code base:** implementation is based on **Threestudio [11]**; the highly optimized GS renderer implementation from [16] is used for rendering. All original 3D Gaussians are trained with methods described in [16].
- **Hardware:** experiments run on a **single RTX A6000 GPU**.
- **3D segmentation speed:** once 2D segmentation masks are obtained (via SAM [18]), segmenting the 3D Gaussians takes **~1 second**.
- **Camera poses:** for large scenes, poses are a subset of the multi-view reconstruction dataset; for targeted objects, poses closely surrounding the segmented object are generated to increase object resolution in rendering. When the target object has low association with the scene, only the target object is rendered to reduce compute. The number of camera poses varies from **24 to 96**.
- **Optimization:** editing typically optimizes **500–1000 steps**, taking **~5–10 minutes** total.
- **Object incorporation:** ~3 min for mesh generation [25] + ~2 min to convert mesh to Gaussians and refine + <1 second for composition.
- **Object removal:** whole procedure ~2 minutes.
- **Note on stated speed ranges:** the main text consistently reports 5–10 min per editing session (Fig. 1, Sec. 1, Sec. 5.1); the supplementary (Fig. 11) reports **2–7 minutes** and **10–20 GB GPU memory** on a single A6000. The discrepancy between 5–10 min and 2–7 min is not reconciled in the paper.

## 4.2 Qualitative Comparisons (Sec. 5.2, Figs. 5, 6)

- Fig. 5 compares Instruct-Nerf2Nerf [12], GaussianEditor-DDS (delta denoising score [14] guidance), and GaussianEditor-iN2N (Instruct-Nerf2Nerf guidance) on prompts such as "Turn him into a clown," "Turn him into Albert Einstein," "Turn him into a Modigliani painting."
- **Claims:**
  - GaussianEditor-iN2N surpasses others in edit quality and controllability.
  - Instruct-Nerf2Nerf produces edits with insufficient detail and cannot control the editing area; the entire scene changes (background and non-target regions affected).
  - GaussianEditor-DDS tends to produce oversaturated colors and less precise edits, because DDS loss [14] is more challenging to control than Instruct-Pix2Pix [4].
  - Gaussian semantic tracing confines edits to target Gaussians (e.g., the whole human body in Fig. 5), keeping non-target regions unchanged.
  - Instruct-Nerf2Nerf's static masks restrict spatial freedom of edits and lose effectiveness as geometries/appearances evolve during training (Sec. 5.2).
- Fig. 6 shows additional scenarios: large-scale scene editing (no semantic tracing used) and facial swaps (face Gaussians traced), keeping backgrounds unchanged.

## 4.3 Quantitative Comparisons (Sec. 5.3, Table 1)

Two metrics are reported: **user study preference (%)** and **CLIP Directional Similarity** (following InstructPix2Pix [4] and StyleGAN-Nada [9]).

| Method | User study | CLIP Directional Similarity |
|---|---|---|
| Instruct-Nerf2Nerf (iN2N) [12] | 15.45% | 0.1600 |
| GaussianEditor-DDS (Ours, DDS) | 12.27% | 0.1813 |
| GaussianEditor-iN2N (Ours, iN2N) | **72.28%** | **0.2071** |

**Verified:** the three user-study percentages sum to exactly 100.00% (15.45 + 12.27 + 72.28), consistent with a single-preference user study. GaussianEditor-iN2N wins both metrics; Ours(DDS) beats iN2N on CLIP similarity but loses on user-study preference (12.27% vs 15.45%).

**Runtime comparison:** Instruct-Nerf2Nerf typically requires **>30 minutes** to edit a scene, while GaussianEditor takes **5–10 minutes** (Sec. 5.3).

## 4.4 Ablation Study (Sec. 5.4, Figs. 7, 8)

Two ablations, both **qualitative only** (no numbers):

1. **HGS ablation (Fig. 7), prompt "make the grass on fire":** without HGS, Gaussians spread and densify across the whole scene (because Instruct-Pix2Pix [4] tends to edit the entire 2D image), causing uncontrolled densification and image blurring; with HGS, this diffusion is restrained by limiting old-generation mobility.
2. **Semantic Tracing ablation (Fig. 8), prompt "Man":** without semantic tracing, edits leak outside the desired region; with tracing, editing is confined to the desired area while the editing region can still expand naturally.

**Summary claim:** HGS limits overall scene mobility; semantic tracing limits editing to a specified area without restricting the expansiveness of the editing region (Sec. 5.4).

## 4.5 Supplementary Results (Appendix)

- **Appendix B:** more qualitative results (Fig. 11) claiming "controllable, diverse, high-resolution 3D editing, needing only 2-7 minutes."
- **Appendix C (WebUI):** thanks to GS's real-time rendering, the WebUI supports **2K resolution at 60fps** (vs. low resolution/frame rates for NeRF-based WebUIs).
- **Appendix C.1 — Semantic tracing with point-based prompts:** users click ~5 points on one view; points are back-projected to 3D (Eq. 9, [x,y,z]ᵀ = [R|t]·z(p)·K⁻¹·[pₓ,p_y,1]ᵀ), re-projected to other views as point prompts for SAM [18], and unprojected back to Gaussians. Enables fine-grained control, e.g., selecting one of multiple same-type objects.
- **Appendix C.2 — Object incorporation with WebUI:** monocular depth estimation [38] can be inaccurate; the WebUI lets users slide a depth-scale control to adjust the size/position of added objects in real time, achieving more accurate alignment.

## 4.6 Evaluation Gaps

- **No standard rendering metrics:** no PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS or any geometric/segmentation accuracy metric is reported; evaluation is based on one user study and CLIP directional similarity.
- **No dataset specification:** scenes used for evaluation are not enumerated; no public benchmark is used or cited.
- **No statistics:** the user study protocol (number of participants, number of questions, variance) and CLIP metric details are not reported.
- **Ablations are qualitative** with no supporting numbers.
- **Baselines limited:** only Instruct-Nerf2Nerf and two self-variants (DDS, iN2N guidance) are compared; NeRF-editing baselines from the related-work section are not quantitatively evaluated.

# 5. Critical Analysis and Strengths/Weaknesses

## 5.1 Strengths

1. **Clear problem framing and targeted fixes.** The paper identifies two concrete, well-documented obstacles specific to GS editing — target-Gaussian identification and instability under stochastic generative guidance — and designs one mechanism per obstacle (semantic tracing; HGS). The design follows directly from the analysis of GS's explicit, non-buffered nature.
2. **Dynamic mask paradigm.** Gaussian semantic tracing (per-Gaussian labels inherited through densification) is a clean solution to the static-mask degradation problem affecting NeRF-based editors [31, 57, 56]. The mask moves with the geometry, and content is allowed to expand freely in space — an advance over spatially locked masks.
3. **Generality of guidance.** By abstracting the 2D guidance as L_Edit = D(Θ; p, e) (Eq. 5), the framework works with both SDS-style and edit-then-train guidance; the paper demonstrates this with two instantiations (iN2N and DDS).
4. **Efficiency as a headline result.** Reported times are an order-of-magnitude improvement over NeRF-based baselines (5–10 min vs >30 min for Instruct-Nerf2Nerf), enabled by GS's real-time rendering and the concatenation-based object-incorporation pipeline (<1 s composition). The interactive WebUI at 2K/60fps is a genuine usability advantage.
5. **Practical tooling.** Point-based prompt tracing (Appendix C.1) and the interactive depth-scale slider (Appendix C.2) address real-world usability issues (disambiguating same-type objects; inaccurate monocular depth) and are validated qualitatively.
6. **Internal consistency of the headline table.** The user-study percentages sum to exactly 100%, and the method that wins the user study also wins CLIP directional similarity, giving the central quantitative claim internal coherence.

## 5.2 Weaknesses / Gaps

1. **Thin quantitative evaluation.** Only two metrics are reported (one table): a user study and CLIP directional similarity. There are **no PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS scores**, no geometry/segmentation accuracy, no public benchmark, and no dataset description. The user study lacks protocol details (participant count, question count, variance, statistical significance).
2. **Ablations are qualitative.** The HGS and semantic-tracing ablations (Figs. 7–8) are image comparisons only, with no numbers quantifying the claimed stabilization or localization benefits.
3. **Missing hyperparameters.** Values for the anchor-loss weights λᵢ (per generation) and λ_P (per property), the densification percentile k%, the semantic-label average-weight threshold, and optimization hyperparameters (learning rates, loss weights) are not reported anywhere, hurting reproducibility.
4. **Inconsistent timing claims.** The main text states 5–10 minutes per editing session, while the supplementary (Fig. 11) states 2–7 minutes; the discrepancy is not explained. Similarly, GS is cited as [15], [16], and [17] in different places (all Kerbl et al. ToG 2023), indicating editorial sloppiness.
5. **Dependency chain risk.** Object incorporation depends on four off-the-shelf components (SDXL inpainting [34], foreground segmentation, Wonder3D [25], DPT depth [38]); failures in any step (especially monocular depth) degrade alignment, and only a manual webUI workaround is offered. No robustness/quantitative alignment analysis is provided.
6. **Limited baselines.** Only Instruct-Nerf2Nerf and two self-variants are compared; several related NeRF-editing methods (e.g., [31, 57]) are discussed but not quantitatively evaluated, weakening the "superior to previous 3D editing methods" claim.
7. **No theoretical grounding.** HGS's stabilization is motivated intuitively ("simulates the buffering function of neural networks") without analysis or guarantees; the anchor-update-at-each-densification rule means anchors are continuously refreshed, so the anchor loss constrains drift relative to recent states rather than the true initial state.
8. **CLIP metric caveat.** CLIP directional similarity rewards prompt-alignment but is known to be insensitive to unintended global changes — precisely the failure mode (whole-scene editing) the paper claims to fix, so the metric may not fully support the controllability claim. No controllability metric (e.g., masked-region fidelity) is reported.

## 5.3 Claims vs. Evidence Check

## Executive Summary

GaussianEditor is the first work to adapt 3D Gaussian Splatting (GS) to the 3D editing task, targeting swift and controllable text-guided editing. The paper's central contributions are (1) **Gaussian semantic tracing** — per-Gaussian semantic tags obtained by unprojecting 2D segmentation masks, inherited through densification, enabling dynamic (rather than static) identification of edit targets throughout training; (2) **Hierarchical Gaussian Splatting (HGS)** — a generational organization of Gaussians with generation-dependent anchor-loss regularization that stabilizes GS optimization under stochastic 2D-diffusion guidance; and (3) a **3D inpainting pipeline** for object removal (~2 min) and object incorporation (~5 min) built on off-the-shelf 2D inpainting, image-to-3D, and depth estimation components. The headline claim is that a single editing session takes 5–10 minutes (supplementary: 2–7 minutes) versus >30 minutes for the NeRF-based baseline Instruct-Nerf2Nerf, with edits confined to target regions.

**Overall assessment:** The paper is strong on problem framing, algorithmic novelty, and demonstrated efficiency/controllability, but its quantitative evaluation is thin (one table: user study + CLIP directional similarity; no PSNR/SSIM, no benchmark dataset, no statistics), ablations are qualitative, and critical hyperparameters (anchor weights, densification percentile, segmentation threshold) are unreported.

## Core Method Summary

- **GS representation (Eqs. 1–4):** each Gaussian has position x, SH color c, opacity α, rotation quaternion q, scale s; rendering via splatting and alpha-blending.
- **Edit loss (Eq. 5):** L_Edit = D(Θ; p, e) — abstracts any 2D diffusion guidance (SDS-style or edit-then-train).
- **Semantic tracing (Eq. 6):** unproject 2D SAM masks to per-Gaussian weights w = Σ o·T·M; label assigned if average weight exceeds a manual threshold; labels inherited by densified children.
- **HGS (Eqs. 7–8):** L = L_Edit + Σ_P λ_P · L_anchor^P, with L_anchor^P = Σᵢ λᵢ(Pᵢ − P̂ᵢ)² over properties {x, s, q, α, c}; λᵢ increases with generation age; densification restricted to top k% gradient Gaussians.
- **Inpainting:** removal = delete + KNN boundary-mask refinement + MSE-supervised repair; incorporation = 2D inpaint (SDXL [34]) → segment → Wonder3D mesh [25] → HGS-refined Gaussians → depth alignment (DPT [38], least squares) → concatenation.

# 1. Paper Overview

## 1.1 Basic Information

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Title** | GaussianEditor: Swift and Controllable 3D Editing with Gaussian Splatting |
| **Authors** | Yiwen Chen\*¹,², Zilong Chen\*³,⁵, Chi Zhang², Feng Wang³, Xiaofeng Yang², Yikai Wang³, Zhongang Cai⁴, Lei Yang⁴, Huaping Liu³, Guosheng Lin\*\*¹,² (\* equal contribution; \*\* corresponding author) |
| **Affiliations** | ¹S-Lab & ²School of CSE, Nanyang Technological University; ³Dept. of CS&T, Tsinghua University; ⁴SenseTime Research; ⁵ShengShu |
| **Venue / Status** | arXiv:2311.14521v4 [cs.CV], 20 Dec 2023 |
| **Project page** | https://buaacyw.github.io/gaussian-editor |
| **Codebase basis** | Threestudio [11]; Gaussian renderer implementation from [16] |

## 1.2 Problem Statement

3D editing is essential in areas such as gaming, virtual reality, and the emerging Metaverse. The paper identifies a fundamental trade-off in prior representations:

- **Traditional explicit representations** (meshes, point clouds) offer interactive editing but fail to realistically depict complex scenes.
- **Implicit representations** (e.g., NeRF [28]) render complex scenes with high fidelity but suffer from slow training/rendering speeds and limited control over specific scene regions (NeRF's MLP encoding restricts direct modification of specific parts, complicates inpainting and scene composition, and hinders practical applications).

**Core research question:** Can a 3D editing algorithm achieve *both* swift, high-fidelity editing *and* precise, controllable area-specific modification? The paper answers this by adapting **3D Gaussian Splatting (GS)** [15] — a real-time-rendering, explicit, point-cloud-like representation — to the 3D editing task for the first time.

## 1.3 Identified Challenges in Editing Gaussian Splatting

The paper identifies three specific challenges that motivate its contributions:

1. **No efficient way to identify target Gaussians.** Precise, controllable editing requires accurately locating the Gaussians to be modified.
2. **Unstable optimization under stochastic generative guidance.** Prior work [7, 44, 52] observed that optimizing GS with highly random guidance such as Score Distillation Sampling [36] is difficult. Because GS is directly exposed to loss randomness (no neural-network buffering), properties of a vast number of Gaussian points are changed each step, resulting in "excessive fluidity" that prevents convergence to fine details.
3. **Object removal/addition is hard.** Simply deleting Gaussians by mask produces artifacts at object-scene interfaces; adding objects requires seamless 3D integration.

## 1.4 Contributions (as stated by the authors)

1. **Gaussian semantic tracing** — enables more detailed and effective editing control by continuously identifying the Gaussians to be edited throughout training (instead of relying on static 2D/3D masks).
2. **Hierarchical Gaussian Splatting (HGS)** — a novel GS representation that converges more stably to refined results under highly random generative guidance by organizing Gaussians into "generations" with generation-dependent anchor constraints.
3. **A dedicated 3D inpainting algorithm for GS** — supports swift object removal and object addition (incorporation).
4. **Extensive experiments** demonstrating superiority over previous 3D editing methods in effectiveness, speed, and controllability.

## 1.5 High-Level Results / Claims

- A single editing session typically takes **5–10 minutes** (and 2–7 minutes for the cases in the appendix), significantly faster than prior NeRF-based editing (Instruct-Nerf2Nerf [12] requires >30 minutes).
- Object removal takes ~**2 minutes**; object incorporation ~**5 minutes** in total.
- GaussianEditor-iN2N wins a user study with **72.28%** preference (vs 15.45% for Instruct-Nerf2Nerf and 12.27% for GaussianEditor-DDS) and achieves the highest CLIP Directional Similarity (**0.2071**).
- Precise editing control: e.g., in "Make the grass on fire", the bench and tree remain unaffected; in face edits, the background remains unchanged.
- The WebUI supports interactive editing at **2K resolution and 60fps**.

# 2. Related Work and Background

## 2.1 3D Representations (Section 2.1 of the paper)

- **NeRF [28]** (groundbreaking implicit representation) enables 3D optimization with only 2D supervision via volumetric rendering, and is widely used in reconstruction [3, 6, 13, 21] and generation [22, 35]. However, NeRF optimization is time-consuming. Acceleration efforts [29, 40] focus on the reconstruction setting (e.g., spatial pruning), which does not effectively speed up the generation setting.
- **3D Gaussian Splatting [15]** has emerged as an alternative to NeRF, showing impressive quality and speed in 3D and 4D reconstruction [15, 26, 47, 50, 51] and attracting interest in generation [7, 44, 52]. Its efficient differentiable rendering implementation and model design enable fast training without spatial pruning.
- **Position of this work:** the authors state they *pioneer the adaptation of 3D Gaussian Splatting to 3D editing tasks*, "harnessing the advantages of this representation for the first time in this context."

## 2.2 3D Editing (Section 2.2 of the paper)

The paper organizes existing 3D editing work into several lines:

1. **Editing neural fields via conditioning** — EditNeRF [24] edits both shape and color of neural fields by conditioning on latent codes.
2. **CLIP-based editing** — works [1, 10, 45, 46] leverage CLIP models for text-prompt or reference-image editing.
3. **Template/skeleton-based methods** — predefined templates or skeletons support re-posing or re-rendering within specific categories [30, 33].
4. **Geometry-based methods** — translate neural fields into meshes and synchronize mesh deformation with implicit fields [20, 48, 49, 54].
5. **2D-manipulation + field training** — combining 2D image manipulation (e.g., inpainting) with neural field training [19, 23].
6. **Static-mask-constrained editing (concurrent works)** — Ed-NeRF [31] and DreamEditor [57] use static 2D/3D masks to constrain the edit area of NeRF. **Limitation identified by the authors:** 3D model training is dynamic; static masks cannot effectively constrain it. In contrast, GaussianEditor employs *Gaussian semantic tracing* to track the target Gaussians throughout the entire training process.

## 2.3 Diffusion-Based Editing Guidance (Section 3.2 of the paper)

Two families of 2D-diffusion-to-3D guidance are distinguished:

- **Type 1 (score-based guidance):** Feed the noised rendering of the current 3D model (plus conditions) into a 2D diffusion model [39]; the generated scores guide model updates. Exemplified by DreamFusion's SDS loss [36]; includes [8, 27, 31, 36, 42, 57]. In this paper, the DDS variant (Delta Denoising Score [14]) is an instance of this type.
- **Type 2 (2D-editing-based guidance):** Perform 2D editing of multiview renderings of the 3D model given prompts, creating a multi-view 2D image dataset used as training target [5, 12, 37, 43]. Instruct-Nerf2Nerf [12] / Instruct-Pix2Pix [4] belong to this family.

The paper deliberately does **not** design a new guidance mechanism; it directly employs the existing guidance methods (denoted generically as the operator D), so that *both* types of guidance can be plugged into GaussianEditor. Two instantiations are evaluated:
- **GaussianEditor-DDS** — uses delta denoising score [14] guidance.
- **GaussianEditor-iN2N** — uses Instruct-Nerf2Nerf [12] (Instruct-Pix2Pix [4]) guidance.

The edit loss is formulated as: **LEdit = D(Θ; p, e)** (Eq. 5), where Θ are the 3D model parameters, p the rendered camera pose, and e the prompt.

## 2.4 Preliminary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (Section 3.1 of the paper)

Key formulas and attributes of the GS representation:

- Each Gaussian is defined by center (mean) **x** and covariance matrix **Σ**:
  **G(x) = e^(−½ xᵀΣ⁻¹x)** (Eq. 1).
- For differentiable optimization, Σ is decomposed into rotation R and scaling S: **Σ = RS Sᵀ Rᵀ** (Eq. 2); gradient flow is detailed in [15].
- For novel-view rendering, splatting [53] positions Gaussians on camera planes. With viewing transform W and Jacobian J of the affine approximation of the projective transform: **Σ′ = J W Σ Wᵀ Jᵀ** (Eq. 3).
- Each Gaussian's attributes: position **x ∈ R³**, color as spherical-harmonics (SH) coefficients **c ∈ Rᵏ** (k = degrees of freedom), opacity **α ∈ R**, rotation quaternion **q ∈ R⁴**, scaling **s ∈ R³**.
- Alpha-blending of N ordered points overlapping a pixel:
  **C = Σᵢ∈N cᵢαᵢ Πⱼ<ᵢ(1−αⱼ)** (Eq. 4), with per-point optimizable opacity and SH color coefficients.

## 2.5 Task Definition (Section 4 of the paper)

The 3D-editing-on-GS task: given a prompt y and a 3D scene Θ (each Θᵢ = {xᵢ, sᵢ, qᵢ, αᵢ, cᵢ}), obtain edited Gaussians **Θy** that align with / adhere to the specification of prompt y.

# 3. Methodology

GaussianEditor's method section (Section 4 of the paper) has three pillars: (i) Gaussian semantic tracing (Sec. 4.1), (ii) Hierarchical Gaussian Splatting / HGS (Sec. 4.2), and (iii) 3D inpainting — object removal and object incorporation (Sec. 4.3). The framework reuses standard GS rendering and diffusion-based guidance (Sec. 3 of the paper) and adds the above mechanisms on top.

## 3.1 Gaussian Semantic Tracing (Section 4.1)

**Motivation.** Prior 3D editing works [31, 57] use static 2D/3D masks to restrict loss to masked pixels. Limitations:
- As the 3D representation changes dynamically during training, static masks become inaccurate or ineffective.
- Static-mask gradient control in NeRF editing confines edits strictly inside the masked area, "locking" the content within a fixed spatial boundary and preventing natural extension beyond the mask.
- Even semantic NeRF [56] is ineffective: gradient control works only at the very beginning of training, since ongoing NeRF updates cause the semantic field to lose accuracy.

**Design.** Because GS is explicit, each Gaussian point can be assigned a semantic label directly. The method:

1. **Add a semantic attribute** to each Gaussian: mᵢⱼ denotes the semantic Gaussian mask for the i-th Gaussian point and j-th semantic label. This enables selectively updating only target Gaussians (precise control).
2. **Semantic inheritance during densification:** newly densified points inherit the semantic label of their parent point, guaranteeing an accurate 3D semantic mask at every moment of training.
3. **Unprojection-based labeling (GS unprojection):** render the Gaussians Θ from multiple viewpoints to produce renderings I; process I with 2D segmentation [18] to get 2D semantic masks M (Mⱼ = j-th semantic label). Then unproject posed 2D semantic labels back to Gaussians via inverse rendering: maintain a weight and a counter per Gaussian; for pixel p on the semantic maps, compute
   **wⁱⱼ = oᵢ(p) · Tⁱⱼ(p) · Mⱼ(p)**   (Eq. 6)
   where wⁱⱼ is the weight of the i-th Gaussian for the j-th semantic label, oᵢ(p) the opacity, Tⁱⱼ(p) the transmittance from pixel p, and Mⱼ(p) the semantic mask of pixel p. A Gaussian is assigned to class j if its average weight exceeds a manually set threshold.
4. **Fast labeling:** the entire labeling process takes less than a second; segmenting the 3D Gaussians (after obtaining 2D masks) takes about 1 second.

**Resulting capabilities** (once the scene is semantically parsed):
- Continuous tracking of each Gaussian's category during training, adapting to evolving properties and numbers.
- Selective application of gradients, densification, and pruning to Gaussians of a specified category.
- Training by rendering only the target object, speeding up editing in complex scenes.
- The semantic mask m acts as a *dynamic* 3D segmentation mask that evolves with training, letting content expand freely in space (unlike NeRF's fixed-area restriction).
- Direct manipulation operations: changing colors, moving properties of a category, deleting categories.
- Small objects: since 2D diffusion guidance often struggles with small objects in complex scenes, target objects can be rendered independently and fed to the 2D diffusion model for more precise supervision.
- A user-interactive extension, *semantic tracing with point-based prompts* (Appendix C.1), supports clicking ~5 points on one view, back-projecting them into 3D (Eq. 9), re-projecting onto other views as point prompts for SAM [18] segmentation, and then unprojecting the semantic maps to Gaussians for finer-grained control.

## 3.2 Hierarchical Gaussian Splatting (Section 4.2)

**Motivation.** Vanilla GS [17] works well for reconstruction because of high-quality SFM [41] point-cloud initialization and stable ground-truth supervision. In generative settings [7, 44, 52], GS is unstable under random generative guidance because:
- GS is directly exposed to the randomness of loss functions (unlike neural-network implicit representations with memorization/moderating ability).
- Each step updates a vast number of Gaussian points; the resulting "excessive fluidity" prevents convergence to detailed results.

**Design — generational organization + anchor loss:**

1. **Generations by densification round:** the initial Gaussians Θ are assigned generation 0; points produced in the k-th densification round are marked generation k.
2. **Generation-dependent constraints:** older generations receive stricter constraints to preserve their original state (reduce mobility); younger generations get fewer/no constraints for adaptability. This moderates GS fluidity while preserving flexibility, simulating the buffering function of neural networks in implicit representations.
3. **Anchor loss:** at training start, HGS records the attributes of all Gaussians as anchors; anchors are updated to reflect current states at each densification process. During training, MSE between anchor state and current state keeps Gaussians near their anchors:
   **Lᵃⁿᶜʰᵒʳ = Σᵢ₌₀ⁿ λᵢ(Pᵢ − P̂ᵢ)²**   (Eq. 7)
   where n = number of Gaussians, P ∈ {x, s, q, α, c} a property of the current Gaussian, P̂ the same property in the anchor state, and λᵢ the anchor-loss strength for the i-th Gaussian (varying by generation).
4. **Overall loss:**
   **L = LEdit + Σ_{P∈{x,s,q,α,c}} λP · Lᵃⁿᶜʰᵒʳ**   (Eq. 8)
   where λP is the anchor-loss strength for property P and LEdit is the edit loss (Eq. 5).
5. **Freezing schedule:** with each densification, the anchor-loss weight λᵢ for all previous generations increases, so the fluidity of existing generations gradually decreases until it nearly solidifies. Stable geometry forms under stochastic losses, while almost-unconstrained Gaussians from new densifications carve out details.
6. **Task-adaptive anchoring:** e.g., increase anchor weight for generation 0 to limit changes to the original GS; apply stronger anchor loss to specific properties (color/geometry) to prevent changing them.
7. **Percentage-based densification:** instead of manually setting a densification threshold, at each densification step only Gaussians whose 3D position gradients are in the top k% are densified — more manageable and intuitive.

## 3.3 3D Inpainting (Section 4.3)

### 3.3.1 Object Removal

- Simply removing Gaussians identified by a mask causes artifacts at interfaces where the object intersects other Gaussians.
- Pipeline: after deletion, use **KNN** to identify Gaussians nearest to the removed ones (likely at the interface); project these onto various views; dilate the mask and fix holes to build a refined mask of boundary zones; use a 2D inpainting method to generate a repaired image, then supervise with **MSE loss**.
- The whole object removal procedure typically takes ~**2 minutes** (Fig. 4).

### 3.3.2 Object Incorporation (Addition)

- Task definition: within Gaussians Θ, given a camera pose p and rendering I from that viewpoint, the user provides a 2D inpainting mask M on I and a prompt y; the system updates Θ to fulfill the inpainting request.
- Pipeline:
  1. Generate a 2D inpainted image **IMy** with a 2D inpainting diffusion model [34].
  2. Segment the foreground object from IMy; feed it to an image-to-3D method [25] to produce a coarse 3D mesh.
  3. Convert the coarse mesh into 3D Gaussians **θy** and refine with HGS (Sec. 4.2).
  4. Estimate the depth of IMy [38]; align it (least squares) with the depth rendered by Θ at pose p to determine the coordinates and scale of the inpainted foreground object in Θ's coordinate system.
  5. Transform θy into Θ's coordinate system and concatenate the two Gaussian sets.
- Timing: ~3 minutes for mesh generation [25], ~2 minutes to transfer to Gaussians and refine, and <1 second for composition — ~5 minutes total (Fig. 3).
- Interactive refinement: the WebUI (Appendix C.2) lets users adjust the estimated depth scale with a slider in real time (only minor position/scale adjustments of a few Gaussians are needed), compensating for inaccurate monocular depth estimates and achieving seamless alignment.

## 3.4 Method Summary Table

| Component | Section | Purpose | Key mechanism |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gaussian semantic tracing | 4.1 | Precise, controllable editing; dynamic target identification | Semantic attribute m; label inheritance on densification; unprojection (Eq. 6); threshold-based assignment |
| Hierarchical Gaussian Splatting (HGS) | 4.2 | Stable convergence under stochastic generative guidance | Generations by densification round; generation-weighted anchor loss (Eqs. 7–8); top-k% densification |
| 3D inpainting: removal | 4.3 | Artifact-free object removal | KNN-based boundary identification; 2D inpaint + MSE supervision |
| 3D inpainting: incorporation | 4.3 | Seamless object addition | 2D inpainting → image-to-3D mesh [25] → HGS refinement → depth alignment (least squares) → concatenation |

# 4. Experiments and Results

## 4.1 Experimental Setup (Section 5.1)

- **Implementation:** uses a highly optimized renderer implementation from [16]; based on Threestudio [11]. All original 3D Gaussians are trained with methods from [16].
- **Hardware:** single RTX A6000 GPU.
- **Segmentation:** 2D segmentation from [18] (SAM); segmenting the 3D Gaussians takes ~1 second (Sec. 4.1).
- **Camera poses:** for large-scene editing, poses are selected from a subset of the multi-view image dataset used for reconstruction; for targeted objects, camera poses closely surround the segmented object to increase resolution in rendering. If the target object has low association with the scene, only the target object is rendered to reduce computational load.
- **Number of camera poses:** varies from 24 to 96 depending on scene complexity.
- **Optimization:** typically 500–1000 steps, 5–10 minutes total, depending on prompt and scene complexity.
- **Object incorporation timing:** ~3 min (mesh via [25]) + ~2 min (transfer to Gaussians + HGS refinement); composition <1 s.
- **Object removal timing:** ~2 minutes total.
- **Appendix (Fig. 11):** 2–7 minutes and 10–20 GB GPU memory on a single A6000.

## 4.2 Qualitative Comparisons (Section 5.2, Fig. 5)

Baselines compared: **Instruct-Nerf2Nerf (iN2N)** [12] and two GaussianEditor variants:
- **GaussianEditor-DDS** — using delta denoising score [14] as guidance.
- **GaussianEditor-iN2N** — using Instruct-Nerf2Nerf [12] (Instruct-Pix2Pix [4]) guidance.

Claimed findings:
- GaussianEditor-iN2N surpasses other methods in both edit quality and controllability.
- Instruct-Nerf2Nerf produces edits with insufficient detail and *cannot control the editing area*; the entire scene undergoes changes, whereas GaussianEditor keeps background/non-target regions essentially unaffected.
- GaussianEditor-DDS tends to produce oversaturated colors and less precise edits because DDS loss [14] is harder to control than Instruct-Pix2Pix guidance.
- GaussianEditor's controllability stems from Gaussian semantic tracing, which identifies target Gaussians at each training step (e.g., the whole human body in Fig. 5).
- Static masks in Instruct-Nerf2Nerf restrict spatial freedom of edits and lose effectiveness as geometry/appearance evolve during training.
- **Versatility (Fig. 6):** the method handles large-scale scenes (no semantic tracing applied) and face swaps / bear edits (semantic tracing applied to the face region), keeping undesired areas unchanged. Example prompts include "Make it snowy", "Make it Autumn", "Turn him into an old lady", "Turn the bear into a grizzly bear".

## 4.3 Quantitative Comparisons (Section 5.3, Table 1)

Metrics: **user study** (preference %) and **CLIP Directional Similarity** [9].

| Method | User study | CLIP Directional Similarity |
|---|---|---|
| Instruct-Nerf2Nerf (iN2N) [12] | 15.45% | 0.1600 |
| GaussianEditor-DDS (Ours) | 12.27% | 0.1813 |
| **GaussianEditor-iN2N (Ours)** | **72.28%** | **0.2071** |

Key claims:
- GaussianEditor-iN2N is superior in both user study and CLIP Directional Similarity.
- Instruct-Nerf2Nerf typically requires >30 minutes per scene; GaussianEditor takes only 5–10 minutes.

## 4.4 Ablation Study (Section 5.4, Figs. 7–8)

Two ablations are reported:

1. **Ablation of HGS (Fig. 7, prompt "make the grass on fire").** Without HGS, Gaussians spread and densify across the whole scene, causing uncontrolled densification and image blurring — because Instruct-Pix2Pix-style generative guidance tends to edit the entire 2D image even when prompts specify an area. HGS restrains this diffusion by constraining the mobility of old-generation Gaussians, so the overall scene does not exhibit excessive mobility.
2. **Ablation of Semantic Tracing (Fig. 8, tracing prompt "Man").** Without semantic tracing, edits spread beyond the desired region. Semantic tracing confines the editing region to the desired area *without restricting the expansiveness of the editing region itself*.

## 4.5 Results on 3D Inpainting (Figs. 3, 4)

- **Object removal (Fig. 4):** naive deletion by semantic mask generates artifacts at the object-scene interface; the 2D-inpainting + MSE supervision pipeline repairs these. Total time ~2 min.
- **Object incorporation (Fig. 3):** given a 2D inpainting mask and a text prompt from a single view ("A Garfield cat on the bench"), the method adds the object at the specified location, with the whole process taking ~5 minutes.

## 4.6 What Is NOT Reported (explicitly noted)

- **No quantitative ablation numbers** for HGS or semantic tracing are given; only qualitative figures (Fig. 7, Fig. 8).
- **No comparison dataset/benchmark specification** beyond the described scenes; the number of scenes used for the user study and CLIP metric computation is not reported.
- **Number of participants in the user study** is not reported.
- **Per-scene hyperparameters** (e.g., exact λᵢ/λP values, top-k% value, the manually set semantic threshold) are not reported in the paper.
- **Statistical significance** of the user-study and CLIP results is not reported.

# 5. Strengths of the Paper

## 5.1 Novelty and Technical Contributions

1. **First adaptation of 3D Gaussian Splatting to 3D editing.** The authors explicitly position GaussianEditor as pioneering GS-based 3D editing ("harnessing the advantages of this representation for the first time in this context"), exploiting GS's real-time rendering and explicit point-cloud-like structure — a timely contribution given GS's rise as an alternative to NeRF.
2. **Gaussian semantic tracing is a genuinely dynamic mask mechanism.** Instead of the static 2D/3D masks used by concurrent NeRF editing works (Ed-NeRF [31], DreamEditor [57]), the semantic attribute m lives on the Gaussians themselves and is inherited by newly densified points. This keeps the mask accurate throughout training and — importantly — does not spatially "lock" the edit, allowing content to expand freely (a limitation of static-mask NeRF editing). The paper argues this point carefully in Sec. 4.1.
3. **Hierarchical Gaussian Splatting (HGS) addresses a real, observed failure mode.** The instability of GS under SDS-like stochastic guidance is documented in prior work [7, 44, 52]. The generation-based anchor loss (Eqs. 7–8) with a progressive freezing schedule is a simple but well-motivated mechanism that mimics the "buffering" that neural networks implicitly provide. The percentage-based (top-k%) densification criterion is a sensible practical improvement over manual thresholds.
4. **A complete, application-oriented editing suite.** Beyond prompt-driven editing, the paper contributes object removal (~2 min), object incorporation (~5 min), and an interactive WebUI (2K @ 60fps) with point-based tracing and depth-scale adjustment — covering the full editing workflow from annotation to final composition.

## 5.2 Experimental Strengths

1. **Both qualitative breadth and quantitative evidence.** The paper shows a wide range of edits (style changes, identity changes, scene-level edits, face edits, object removal/addition) and supplements them with a user study plus CLIP Directional Similarity (Table 1).
2. **Two guidance variants tested (DDS and iN2N).** Because the framework is guidance-agnostic, the paper demonstrates compatibility with both major families of 2D-diffusion guidance, and shows that the choice of guidance matters (iN2N variant outperforms DDS variant).
3. **Head-to-head comparison with Instruct-Nerf2Nerf.** The comparison is meaningful because it isolates the contribution of the GS representation + tracing/HGS from the underlying 2D guidance: GaussianEditor-iN2N and Instruct-Nerf2Nerf use the same 2D editing guidance, yet GaussianEditor achieves markedly better controllability and user preference (72.28% vs 15.45%).
4. **Speed is a headline, well-quantified result.** 5–10 minutes per editing session (vs >30 min for Instruct-Nerf2Nerf), ~2 min for removal, ~5 min for incorporation, <1 s labeling, <1 s composition — these concrete numbers substantiate the "swift" claim.
5. **Targeted ablations.** Each of the two core components (HGS, semantic tracing) is ablated qualitatively (Figs. 7–8), demonstrating that removing either component leads to the predicted failure mode (scene-wide blurring; edits spreading outside the target region).

## 5.3 Writing and Presentation Strengths

1. **Clear problem framing.** The paper crisply articulates why GS editing is hard (target identification; instability under stochastic guidance; interface artifacts) and maps each challenge to a dedicated contribution.
2. **Well-structured motivation chain.** Related work and preliminary sections (Secs. 2–3) set up the representation and guidance taxonomy that the method section builds upon.
3. **Effective visual communication.** Figures 1–8 directly support the claimed controllability (e.g., "Make the grass on fire" leaves the bench and tree untouched; face edits leave backgrounds unchanged).
4. **Honest limitation statement.** The authors acknowledge dependence on 2D diffusion models and that current 2D diffusion models struggle with complex prompts, limiting 3D editing quality.

# 6. Weaknesses, Limitations, and Critiques

## 6.1 Limitations Acknowledged by the Authors

1. **Dependence on 2D diffusion models.** GaussianEditor relies on 2D diffusion models for supervision. Current 2D diffusion models struggle to provide effective guidance for certain complex prompts, limiting 3D editing quality (Conclusion, Limitation paragraph).
2. **Dependence on auxiliary components.** The pipeline depends on 2D segmentation [18], 2D inpainting [34], image-to-3D [25], and monocular depth estimation [38] — each is an error source (e.g., the paper itself notes that monocular depth estimates are not always accurate and require manual WebUI correction, Appendix C.2). The paper also notes that initial 2D segmentation masks can be inaccurate, though Gaussian semantic tracing is designed to remain robust to this (Fig. 2 caption).
3. **2D diffusion guidance struggles with small objects in complex scenes** — although the paper proposes rendering target objects independently as a mitigation (Sec. 4.1), the underlying limitation of the guidance signal remains.

## 6.2 Methodological Weaknesses / Critique

1. **Ablations are qualitative only.** The ablation study (Sec. 5.4, Figs. 7–8) provides visual evidence but no quantitative ablation numbers (no CLIP/user-study scores for the without-HGS and without-tracing variants). This weakens the claim that HGS and semantic tracing are strictly necessary for the quantitative gains in Table 1.
2. **Limited quantitative protocol detail.** The paper does not report: the number of scenes in the evaluation, the number of user-study participants, per-scene breakdowns, or statistical significance tests. The user study is a single aggregate preference percentage (Table 1).
3. **Single-metric CLIP Directional Similarity.** Quantitative evaluation rests on one CLIP-based metric plus a user study; there are no fidelity metrics (e.g., reference-based LPIPS/PSNR vs. the original scene in unchanged regions) to substantiate the "background remains unchanged" claims numerically.
4. **No comparison with a wider set of baselines.** The quantitative comparison is limited to Instruct-Nerf2Nerf and the authors' own two variants; concurrent GS-generation/editing works [7, 44, 52] and other NeRF editing methods (e.g., DreamEditor [57], Ed-NeRF [31]) are discussed but not quantitatively compared.
5. **Hyperparameters are not fully specified.** The anchor-loss weights λᵢ (per generation) and λP (per property), the top-k% densification criterion, and the semantic assignment threshold are described qualitatively ("manually set threshold," "increase the anchor loss weight") without concrete values, which limits reproducibility.

2. **User-study preference gap may partly reflect representation, not components.** The large gap between GaussianEditor-iN2N (72.28%) and Instruct-Nerf2Nerf (15.45%) could stem from GS's rendering quality itself; the isolated contribution of semantic tracing and HGS to the quantitative metrics is not directly measured.

# 8. Conclusion and Summary Assessment

## 8.1 Summary of the Paper

GaussianEditor is the first 3D editing algorithm built on 3D Gaussian Splatting (GS). It addresses three obstacles to GS-based editing with three matching contributions:

1. **Gaussian semantic tracing** (Sec. 4.1) assigns each Gaussian a semantic label (via unprojection of 2D segmentation masks with opacity/transmittance weighting, Eq. 6), inherits labels to newly densified points, and thereby provides a *dynamic* 3D editing mask that stays accurate throughout training and does not spatially lock the edit region.
2. **Hierarchical Gaussian Splatting (HGS)** (Sec. 4.2) organizes Gaussians into generations by densification round and applies generation-weighted anchor losses (Eqs. 7–8), progressively freezing older Gaussians while letting new densifications carve details — stabilizing GS optimization under stochastic 2D-diffusion guidance.
3. **3D inpainting for GS** (Sec. 4.3) provides object removal (~2 min, KNN-identified boundary repair with 2D-inpainting + MSE supervision) and object incorporation (~5 min, 2D inpainting → image-to-3D mesh [25] → HGS refinement → least-squares depth alignment → Gaussian concatenation), complemented by an interactive WebUI (2K @ 60fps) with point-based tracing and depth-scale correction.

The evaluation (Sec. 5) shows that GaussianEditor-iN2N (Instruct-Nerf2Nerf guidance on GS) wins a user study with 72.28% preference and the highest CLIP Directional Similarity (0.2071) among Instruct-Nerf2Nerf (15.45%, 0.1600) and GaussianEditor-DDS (12.27%, 0.1813), while completing edits in 5–10 minutes versus >30 minutes for Instruct-Nerf2Nerf. Qualitative results demonstrate precise area control (grass-on-fire, face swaps, bear edits) and qualitative ablations confirm the roles of HGS (prevents scene-wide blurring) and semantic tracing (confines edits to target regions).

## 8.2 Balanced Verdict

**Strengths.** Timely and well-motivated problem framing; three clean, reusable technical contributions (dynamic semantic masks for explicit representations, generation-based anchor losses, GS-specific inpainting); a guidance-agnostic framework validated with two guidance families; strong qualitative evidence of controllability; concrete and compelling speed numbers; and an application-complete pipeline (removal, addition, WebUI).

**Weaknesses.** Quantitative evaluation is thin in protocol detail (no scene counts, participant counts, or significance tests); ablations are qualitative only; hyperparameters (λᵢ, λP, top-k%, semantic threshold) are unspecified, limiting reproducibility; quantitative comparison covers only one external baseline; the depth-aligned concatenation for object incorporation is not evaluated for seam quality or cross-view consistency.

**Overall assessment.** GaussianEditor is a significant and influential contribution to 3D editing: it demonstrated that explicit Gaussian representations can support controllable, swift, diffusion-guided editing, introduced mechanisms (semantic unprojection, generational anchor losses) that generalize beyond the paper, and set speed/interactivity as central evaluation criteria. Its evidence base would be stronger with quantitative ablations, fuller protocol details, and broader baseline comparison. Within the scope of what it claims — swift, controllable, versatile 3D editing — the paper is convincing; the main caveat is the acknowledged dependence on the capabilities of the underlying 2D diffusion models.
